big_idea: On bigger data, ONE bar height = TWO or FIVE or TEN units. SCALE matters!
learning_intention: We are learning to use many-to-one scale on a bar graph.
student_learning_goal: I can use many-to-one scale on a bar graph.
lesson_specific_materials: OPTIONAL: Detective Dot and Tally — if available; otherwise teacher voices both characters in two distinct voices, or substitutes two stuffed animals / paper-bag puppets / pictures on the anchor poster. Activity is unaffected.
Scaled Bar Graph Grid (1 per pair)

minds_on.hook: Detective Dot: 30 students like hockey. The bar would be HUGE! Let's use SCALE — 1 unit = 5 students. Bar = 6 units! Dot opens: 'CHECK the scale, MULTIPLY the height — that's the COUNT!'
minds_on.teacher_script:
Bring children to the carpet. Detective Dot and Tally puppets. 'Friends — yesterday frequency tables. Today MANY-TO-ONE SCALE.'

Introduce vocabulary. Write SCALE on chart. 'Scale = how much each bar unit shows. 1 unit = 1 child (one-to-one), or 1 unit = 5 children (many-to-one).'

Demonstrate. Show data: 30 hockey, 15 soccer, 10 basketball, 5 baseball.

'One-to-one would need bars 30, 15, 10, 5 units high — too tall!'

Now many-to-one. 'Pick scale: 1 unit = 5 children.' Recompute: 6, 3, 2, 1. 'Bars now fit on a normal grid.'

Draw the y-axis: 0, 5, 10, 15, 20, 25, 30. Bars at the right heights.

'Detective Dot says — when data is BIG, pick a scale. 1 unit = 5 (or 10, or 2). LABEL the scale on the y-axis.'

More scale examples (Canadian flavour):
- 100 students surveyed. Scale: 1 unit = 10. Bars 1-10.
- 50 students. Scale: 1 unit = 5. Bars 1-10.
- 12 students. Scale: 1 unit = 2. Bars 1-6.

'Detective Dot says — pick scale to FIT the grid. Mark scale on y-axis.'

Read a scaled graph. 'Bar at 4 units. Scale 1=5. So 4 × 5 = 20 children.'

'Today YOU build scaled bar graphs.'

steps.instruction: Whole group: scale a 30-student data set.
Three stations. A: Read scaled bar (1 unit = 5). B: Build from frequency table (50 students, scale = 5). C: Pick scale for new data set.
Stretch at C: explain why scale matters.

steps.teacher_prompt: Show: too small scale → giant bars. Too big → tiny bars.

steps.instruction: INVENT-AND-COMPARE: At Station C, pairs design TWO different scales for the same 50-student data (1 unit = 5 vs 1 unit = 10). Class compares: which is more readable? Cite Friel, Curcio & Bright (2001) intermediate level — scale choice matters.
steps.teacher_prompt: Dot: 'Different scale, same data, different graph. Pick the scale that fits your biggest count.'

differentiation.for_movement_learners: Children form bar graph lines using their bodies; teacher labels.

formative_check.what_to_look_for: Three signals: picks scale; reads scaled bars; builds scaled bars.

discussion_prompts: How do we read a scaled bar?
consolidation.exit_routine: Detective Dot's scale refrain — 'CHECK the scale, MULTIPLY the height — that's the COUNT!' (3x). Each child reads one bar with scale-aware total.

expanded_walkthrough.title: When the child reads SCALED bar as 1-to-1 — repairing the scale-blind trap at Grade 3
expanded_walkthrough.rationale:
On many-to-one bar graphs, the trap is the scale-blind error: child reads bar height as count when 1 unit = 5 students. Friel, Curcio & Bright (2001) graph-comprehension hierarchy (elementary/intermediate/advanced) places scale-aware reading at intermediate level — Grade-3 children must transition there.

Yesterday Tally tabulated frequencies. Today scale converts table rows to graph bars. Lesson 4 mean/mode; Lesson 5 capstones.
expanded_walkthrough.setup: Pair at A. Bar graph with scale 1 unit = 5. Bar at 4 units. Child reports '4 children'.
expanded_walkthrough.teacher_script:
Crouch. 'You said 4. Detective Dot asks — what does the SCALE say?'

Guide. 'Look at y-axis: 0, 5, 10, 15, 20. So 4 units = 4 × 5 = 20 children.'

Generlise. 'Detective Dot says — always READ the scale first. Bar height × scale = real count.'

If still scale-blind: provide a 'scale check' card to read first.
expected_student_responses: (Stretched) Uses different scales for different data sets.
common_misconceptions: Bar height = count. (Repair: bar height × scale = count.)
Scale doesn't matter. (Repair: always check scale.)
recovery_moves: DIAGNOSTIC A — child reads bar height literally (height = count): drill 'CHECK the scale — 1 unit = ___'; child re-reads with scale multiplier.
DIAGNOSTIC B — child uses scale but multiplies wrong: physical demo — count grid units, multiply by scale factor.
DIAGNOSTIC C — child can read but cannot construct: drill 'pick scale FIRST based on biggest count, then plot.'

parts_outline.task: Read a scaled bar graph (1 unit = 5). Find counts for 4 categories.
Build a scaled bar graph from a frequency table.
Pick scale for 3 different data sets.
